@graph.description: Map human-readable labels to symbolic labels [a_i], insert <unk> to separate hierarchy levels, and reverse order from children to parents.
@graph.anchor: Rather, we replace the original labels with symbolic labels.
@graph.context:
Rather, we replace the original labels with symbolic labels. For example, the symbolic label [a_14] represents the label “Top/Classifieds/Job Market/Job Categories/Media, Entertainment and Publishing” in the NYT dataset as shown in Figure 2.

The label tokenizer’s vocabulary consists of the set of symbolic labels of the dataset.

@graph.description: Tokenize symbolic labels into fixed-size sequences with <s>, </s>, <pad>, and <unk> tokens.
@graph.anchor: The tokenizer uses the <s> and </s> tokens to mark the beginning and end of the label sequence.
@graph.context:
The tokenizer uses the <s> and </s> tokens to mark the beginning and end of the label sequence. It also uses the <pad> token to fill the rest of the vector after the </s> token. In addition, the <unk> token separates hierarchy levels.

The label tokenizer’s vocabulary consists of the set of symbolic labels of the dataset.

@graph.name: RADAr
@graph.description: Sequence-to-sequence architecture using RoBERTa encoder and autoregressive decoder for hierarchical text classification.
@graph.anchor: RADAr (Transformer-based Autoregressive Decoder Architecture)
@graph.context: In this paper, we introduce an effective hierarchical text classifier RADAr (Transformer-based Autoregressive Decoder Architecture) that is based only on an off-the-shelf RoBERTa transformer to process the input and a custom autoregressive decoder with two decoder layers for generating the classification output.

@graph.name: RADAr (RoBERTa-base encoder)
@graph.description: RADAr model with RoBERTa-base encoder and 2-layer transformer decoder over symbolic label sequences.
@graph.anchor: Any encoder-only model can be used as the encoder of RADAr, but we choose to use RoBERTa base.
@graph.context:
RADAr is a transformer-based encoder-decoder model. Any encoder-only model can be used as the encoder of RADAr, but we choose to use RoBERTa base. The decoder is an autoregressive transformer-based model trained from scratch to generate a sequence of labels.

Using the WOS dataset, we conducted pre-experiments regarding the number of decoder layers and the features of its transformer blocks [36]. We observe that the optimal choice is when the decoder has two decoder layers. Each layer has a transformer block with eight attention heads, a feedforward network and uses a dropout of 0.2.

@graph.name: Autoregressive label-sequence decoder with greedy search
@graph.description: Autoregressive transformer decoder over symbolic label tokens using greedy search until end-of-sequence token.
@graph.anchor: The decoder is an autoregressive transformer-based model
@graph.context: The decoder is an autoregressive transformer-based model whose vocabulary corresponds to the label set. As such, the decoder’s vocabulary is limited to the symbolic labels [28], i.e., internal label identifiers and special tokens (see Figure[2]). Our decoder iteratively uses the previously generated tokens and the encoder’s output as condition to generate the next token. It uses greedy search that picks the token with the highest probability at each decoding step without considering future consequences [39]. It stops when it reaches the special token <s>, indicating the end of the sequence.

@graph.name: Batch-level focal loss optimization
@graph.description: Batch-level cross-entropy scaled with focal loss (γ=2) to emphasize hard batches with rare labels.
@graph.anchor: we employ a batch-level focal loss [21]
@graph.context:
The labels in HTC datasets are typically very imbalanced [35]. To compensate for this imbalance, we employ a batch-level focal loss [21], i.e., the model aims to optimize batches that are hard to classify.

We use focal loss with focusing parameter γ = 2 as described in Section 3. Focal loss depends on cross-entropy with label smoothing of 0.1.

We use the AdamW optimizer [23] with default settings and learning rates of 5 · 10−5 and 3 · 10−4 for the encoder and decoder, respectively.

@graph.name: encoder_learning_rate

@graph.context:
During training, we use the AdamW optimizer [23] with default settings and learning rates of 5 · 10−5 and 3 · 10−4 for the encoder and decoder, respectively.

For example, 5 · 10−5 is known to be a reasonable learning rate for RoBERTa [10], so we specify the range [5 · 10−4, 5 · 10−6] to contain that value.
